utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all, we had a late start because the Chamber who occupied this courtroom had to finish up a witness. Second, a matter that should be clearly on the record, Prosecution Exhibit 295, yesterday if it is not clear on the record, it should be clear that it is admitted under seal. Third, the Chamber would like to respond at this stage to the request by the Stanisic Defence to put questions to Dr. Eekhof. The Chamber allows the Stanisic Defence to put questions to Dr. Eekhof in writing. After answers have been received, the Chamber will determine whether there is any need to seek further information than to be given orally by Dr. Eekhof. The Prosecution's argument that it's premature to put questions to Dr. Eekhof prior to the filing of a request for provisional release is rejected. The Prosecution may also formulate questions for Dr. Eekhof to answer which could be relevant for future consideration of provisional release. The Chamber requires the Stanisic Defence to reformulate its questions. The Chamber is concerned by the questions in which matters are raised which fall outside the scope of the expertise of Dr. Eekhof in which sometimes no clear distinction is drawn between facts known and still unknown, existent facts, future facts, and in which it is not always clear what medical expertise could provide us with in respect to those facts. As guidance for the reformulation, the Chamber states following: Questions should focus on changes in circumstances that occurred since December, that is to say since the last decision of the Chamber in respect of provisional release. New facts should be clearly described, not vaguely addressed in the context of possible consequences which they may result in. A clear distinction should be made between facts which are and which are not of a primarily medical character. Medical conclusions should not be asked for if it is obvious that reasonably no answer could be expected which could meaningfully assist the Chamber, or if they at first sight impress as calling for speculative answers. Composite questions are to be avoided to the extent possible. Before the Chamber allows questions to be passed on to Dr. Eekhof, the Chamber will review those questions. Now, I give you finally two examples, one of a question which is totally appropriate to put to Dr. Eekhof, and another one which would not be appropriate to be put to Dr. Eekhof. I'll start with the inappropriate question. Inappropriate would be a question, Could you quantify the effect of continuing the colitis treatment in Belgrade on a poly-clinical basis together with the possible improvement of the state of depression of Mr. Stanisic in terms of the risks that he would be declared unfit to travel back? This is an exaggeration, I am aware of that, but, therefore, perhaps you should focus more on the question that could be appropriately put to Dr. Eekhof. Has the development of the thrombosis in the leg of Mr. Stanisic in the last few weeks been of such nature that it would be a medical obstacle for a flight of approximately three or four hours in the near future? That is a question that could appropriately be put to Dr. Eekhof. Of course, there is a whole range in between, but the Chamber will look very critical at the questions and relevant concrete information which assists is certainly to be sought; however, vague and speculative material is to be avoided. That, as far as the guidance is concerned. If there's no other matter, we could establish whether the videolink is functioning well and hear the evidence of the next witness for which no protective measures are sought. Mr. Groome? Or should I immediately address Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Friedman will be handling Mr. Sutalo, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then let us establish whether the videolink is functioning well. Could I address the representative of the Registry in the location of the videolink and could I inquire, first of all, whether you can see us well and whether you can hear us well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon Your Honours. Yes, we can see and hear you well in the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true in the opposite direction, we can see and hear you. Could you tell us who are in the room apart from the persons we see, that is, two representatives of the Registrar and what appears to be the witness of this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] There is also a technician in the room, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would like it to address the witness. I do understand it to be Mr. Sutalo. Can you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Sutalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is now handed out to you. If you would please stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Sutalo. Mr. Sutalo, you will first be examined by Ms. Friedman. Ms. Friedman is counsel for the Prosecution, and you will see her soon on your screen. Ms. Friedman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sutalo.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement in this case in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter number 5254 be placed on the monitor and shown to the witness. This is a 92 bis package which includes a statement dated the 17th of April, 1999, as well as addendum dated 18 June 2003. Once again as with JF-017, Your Honours, the B/C/S statement was given paragraph numbers at the time that the addendum was made for the sake of clarity of the addendum. And the Prosecution, therefore, seeks leave to use a numbered version of the English statement in the translation of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the position of the parties is the same as it was in relation to the witness with whom we had a similar issue. Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would ask that we first look at the statement dated the 17th of April, 1999, which is the 5th page in the B/C/S version of the 92 ter package and the third page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, do you recognise this as your statement from 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And would you please look at the signatures on the bottom of the page. Do you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could the court usher please go to page number 10 of both the B/C/S and English versions. In terms of the e-court page number, that's 14 in the B/C/S and 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sutalo, do you recognise any signatures here as well?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Which signature do you recognise, meaning whose signature?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: They are mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity prior to testifying today to review the translation of this statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is a lot of background noise, we are finding it hard to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that background noise in the videolink, or does it come from here? Then, perhaps it is caused by the papers, or is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, the paperers, I believe the microphone on the table is amplifying the sound of the paper rustling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then the papers are to be kept as far away -- rather not move the microphone, but move the papers. That might better assist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When we reviewed your statement last week, was there anything that you wished to change or clarify?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you recall, I would like to take you to certain parts of your statement and see if after hearing me read it back to you whether there is indeed anything that you wish to change. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of your 1999 statement discusses the 1st of August, 1991, and states as follows: "The mayor of Osijek came on the radio telling all soldiers to go defend Dalj." Do you have any corrections to make to that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. Only when I was there in Serbia for interrogation or questioning, the main commander of the Yugoslav Army told me that that is what he had heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, the first sentence of paragraph 10 of this statement reads: "A third group of tanks, again about 50 in number, came and entered Erdut." Do you have any corrections to make to that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall how many tanks entered your village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I know just five or six. At that time there weren't more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So if you saw a group of 50 passing by on the way to Erdut, would you say that -- is it your evidence now that only several of them, five to six entered Erdut and the others passed by in the direction of Dalj?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 11 of your statement describes your detention in a factory in Vojvodina. You state that there were two other men who you recognised and you state: "One was Zvonko Tucak from Erdut and the other was called Mata, I don't remember his family name. He was from Dalj." Is there anything you wish to change to that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: He worked in Dalj, but he was originally from Sonda [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 21 when describing the situation in Erdut after the take-over of the JNA forces, you state: "A curfew was imposed and every single street in Erdut had a check-point manned by JNA soldiers." Is there anything you wish to change?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: This was not the JNA. This was some kind of Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 33 when discussing your interrogation while you were imprisoned at the police station in Dalj, you state: "I learned from others imprisoned with me that the person asking the questions was Colonel Milorad Stricevic" -- sorry, "... was called Milorad Stricevic and that he was a colonel." Is there anything you wish to change?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. He wasn't a colonel, they just called him colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 37 when you discuss being transferred to the Borovo police station you state: "Here we were put into a basement that contained approximately half a metre of water." Is there anything you wish to clarify?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you describe what kind of water was in this basement?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: This was water from the sewer. It stank to high heaven in that room. You couldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I will ask for the final clarification, which is in paragraph 47. When describing your release from the Dalj police station, which we will talk about in greater detail later in your testimony, you state that the man who was being referred to as

utterances.speaker: MR. PRESIDENT
utterances.text: "Said to some soldiers, I'm taking Sutalo, and you will Palinkas to Aljmas to his house. I will look after it." Do you wish to clarify here the word "soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: He didn't say that to soldiers, but to policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And other than this, is there anything in your statement that you wish to change at this time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you are going to ask me. When we go through things further, then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you do recall, however, that we reviewed this statement last week in your home?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, we have -- now we've gone through several parts of your statement. Is there anything that comes to mind that you remember that was written in the statement that you did not agree with which we haven't discussed already today?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I really didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And could the court usher please now turn to the addendum which is page 4 in the B/C/S of the package and page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, the document before you purports to be an addendum to your statement. And it is dated 18 June, 2003. Do you recognise any signatures on it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I do. It's my signature too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And prior to your testimony today, did you have a chance to review this addendum in your own language?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Are there any changes you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, no changes. It was Loncarevic, and it probably still is today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you are referring to the changes that are already noted there on the addendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now that you have taken today the solemn declaration and with the corrections and clarifications that you have made in court today, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of both your 1999 statement and 2003 addendum?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today as you were asked when preparing these documents, would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: This latest that we have is what it is. I didn't even know him at the time. I don't know how it happened that it's not Loncarevic but Loncevic, I don't know, but, anyway, I do know that he is Loncarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 5254, which is the 92 bis package of this witness dated 18 June 2003, which contains both the statement and addendum into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, before we proceed, Mr. Sutalo, your last answer I understood that to be that apart from this one matter of a name, that you would give the same answers in substance if the same questions would be put to you again with all the corrections you've made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am saying that it's Loncarevic and not Loncaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And all the rest would remain the same as far as your answers are concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05254 shall be given Exhibit P00301. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The package of two statements and to which number P301 is assigned is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, the Prosecution also tenders 65 ter 40 which is an associated exhibit to the witness's 92 ter package. This Exhibit contains photographs which are actually video stills that were shown to the witness and are referred to in the last two paragraphs of his 1999 statement. The witness was originally shown colour versions of these photos, but unfortunately the quality of the photos when they were scanned into the 92 bis package is rather poor. I've obtained the better colour copies and have shown them to both Defence teams. They have agreed for these photos to be tendered as 65 ter 40 rather than the poorer quality ones. I also note that these colour photos bear the original ERN which was scanned into the package as well as the ERN corresponding to the better copies. For the convenience of the Chamber and Defence counsel, I've prepared a chart that lists the photos with the two sets of ERNs, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you are seeking the photographs together as one package to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, just the good copy with the chart if you so wish for your convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the chart, so 65 ter would then contain the photographs and the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number to the set of photographs and the chart contained in 65 ter number 40.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The set of photographs also referred to as 65 ter 40 as well as the chart shall be uploaded as Exhibit number P00302. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P302 has been admitted into evidence. Has it been uploaded already?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then the decision on admission is now final. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, do you recall giving testimony before this Tribunal and the 28th of August, 2003, in the Slobodan Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when we met in preparation for your testimony today, did you have an opportunity to listen to the audio recordings of your testimony in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Having reviewed your testimony, is there anything that you wish to change?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you today affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today as you were asked then, would you provide the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 5256 which is the prior testimony this witness given in the case against Slobodan Milosevic on 28 August, 2003, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Not. Ms. Friedman, have you carefully verified any repetitious elements in that testimony compared to the statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that testimony is rather brief. It contains mostly a summary of the witness with a few clarification questions. It was done pursuant to the 92 bis procedure, whereby it was mainly cross-examination. So it's a short examination by the Prosecution, some cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic, and that cross-examination does cover other areas while the summary is somewhat duplicative, but it is very brief, so for the completeness of the record, we submit it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, since there are no objections, the testimony of in Milosevic, Mr. Registrar, would receive what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 5256 shall be admitted as Exhibit P00303. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P303 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now that the witness's prior evidence has been tendered pursuant to 92 ter, would I like to read a summary of that evidence for the benefit of the public. Mr. Sutalo, please listen as I read this summary. Mr. Luka Sutalo is an ethnic Croat who lived in the village of Erdut in 1991. He provides evidence about the rising tensions in 1990 and 1991 and the take-over of Erdut on the 1st of August 1991. Immediately after the take-over, Mr. Sutalo tried to escape to Serbia. However, when he crossed the border, he was arrested, detained, and interrogated before being returned to Erdut. He described the conditions subsequent to the take-over, which included a curfew, restrictions on movement, looting, forced labour, and repeated interrogation by the police. Mr. Sutalo describes being imprisoned for about one month beginning on the 25th of August, in several different locations. He was first taken to the Dalj police station, then a collection centre in Borovo Selo, next the Borovo Selo police station, and finally he was returned to the Dalj police station. Mr. Sutalo states that it was when he was returned to the Dalj police station that, in his words, "the real horror began." Many of the prisoners were constantly beaten and forced to do labour. While Mr. Sutalo was imprisoned in the Dalj police station, he saw Arkan accompanied by three of his men enter the prison, introduce himself, and watch as his men severely beat the prisoners. Mr. Sutalo describes how in late September, he was released from the Dalj police station by Goran Hadzic personally. As they left the police building, Mr. Sutalo saw 30 to 40 Chetniks in front of the yard, including Arkan. Mr. Sutalo learned that another man who was imprisoned with him, Slavko Palinkas was also released that same day, but he never saw the rest of the prisoners again. Mr. Sutalo was eventually granted a permit to leave Erdut in February 1992 after signing over his house and all of his property to the village council.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, what I have read is only a summary, it does not serve as your actual evidence in this case. But I want to make sure that it is accurate. So my question to you is whether anything I've said is a mischaracterisation or a misstatement of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, it is as you read it. It was like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will ask you a few more questions today. In paragraph 19 of your 1999 statement, you describe attending a meeting where a form of new local government was elected which included members of all three ethnic groups; Serbs, Croats, and Hungarians. You stated: "Present and in charge of the meeting which lasted about half an hour was Colonel Kosutic who said at the outset that we were there to elect representatives of government, that it wasn't democratic but that it would have to act in a democratic way." So my question to you is whether there were any subsequent meetings involving all three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: There were a number of meetings but no Croats or Hungarians attended them, only Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the Colonel Kosutic that you referred to, was he the same man that questioned you when you were detained in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Had you seen him ever in Erdut before that day?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, on one more occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember when that occasion was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That was some seven or eight days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So before the meeting on the 5th of August, you did not see him in Erdut, is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I did see him later on, but not before that. Just the time when he questioned me in Bogojevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 you refer to another man at the meeting, Marko Loncarevic who you believe was from Dalj, and you state: "He made a speech and said that this was not Croatia anymore, it was now Serbia, and that the Croat people would not rule anymore and no longer be part of the government." In addition to that --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In addition to that, do you recall anything else that was said that this Loncarevic said?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, just that he said that it was no longer Croatia and that the wheat that was in Erdut, that it would be taken to Serbia and not to Osijek, which was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 22, you state: "The JNA had their military command HQ in Erdut at my son Dobrislav's house." And did your son offer his house to them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, he was in Germany at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How did they come to be in his house then?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I had the keys to his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: And a lieutenant came and said that I had to hand over the keys. I tried not to, but under pressure, finally, I had to give it to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did soldiers move into other houses as well?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, they moved in into all the Croatian homes that were empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did anyone other than soldiers move into the homes?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Not in our place, but, yes, in the village because Arkan's men arrived there, and they had a camp for military training, and the Arkan's men moved in there, in other words, Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I would like to talk to you now about your detention in the Dalj police station in greater detail. Firstly, did you know the men who were the police officers in Dalj before the war?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No. At the Dalj police station, there were Croat policemen, but then on the 1st of August, those police officers were killed by them, and later on I didn't see any of them except Cizmic, I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So just to be clear, the Croat police officers who were in the police station before the war were people that you knew and would have been able to recognise?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: When Yugoslavia broke up, Serbs left their jobs, then Croats put in their place their own police officers, but then when the Yugoslav Army returned, then they shot them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And can you describe for us how you came to be released from the Dalj police station?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I was in detention there when Hadzic [realtime transcript read in error "Adzic"] came, the Krajina commander, and he released me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you were -- were you accompanied by him when you exited -- when you left the building?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, and his company. He wasn't the only one there. There was another man. When he came, I was lying down. So when he entered, he asked, Which one of you is Sutalo? And I said that that was me. And then he said, Well, get ready, you are coming with me, I'm taking you home. And at that point, Palinkas also pleaded with him to let him go too. He said, Why should I stay here with these young men, why don't you let me come along with this -- with me. So then he released him too. And then we came to the police station. There was only one police officer there, a Serb, and he asked -- he asked for my file then, and then he replied, Sutalo doesn't have a file. And then the other guy just swore at him and said, So how can you keep a man in prison when there is no file? And then he said, Mr. President, I don't know who is keeping him in prison; it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when you then left the building with Hadzic accompanying you, you gave evidence that there were these Chetniks outside the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When we left the police station, I saw some 30 to 40 Chetniks outside, and then somebody yelled, Be still, and then they actually reported, there was an officer to whom they reported. And then I don't know what happened next, but I saw Arkan among them, and then he said, Sutalo, just come with me, I'm taking you home. And that's how he took me home.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay, and when you say "he," I take it you are referring to Goran Hadzic. And my question was whether the people outside the building acknowledged --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And my question is whether the people outside the building acknowledged this Goran Hadzic in any way?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, oh, yes. As I said, they reported to him. They -- it was like a review of troops, then he went up to the troops and according to whatever their laws were, they handed him something over. I don't know what it was, I wasn't close enough. But basically they just greeted him with honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when you use the term "Chetniks," what do you mean by that phrase?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I mean Arkan's men. They were young boys who said -- who told stories about how they had been released from juvenile facilities, detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You described at paragraph 56 of your statement that you were told by Palinkas, the other man who was released after you, that he actually returned to the prison after being released in order to give his cigarettes to the remaining prisoners. And you state: "On reaching the prison and speaking to the guard, he was told that there were no prisoners left." Can you tell us if you remember exactly what Palinkas told you about this conversation with the guard?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: When he came with me to the police station, Hadzic said that he was taking me home and that they should take Palinkas to his home. Then when he set off to go home, on the way, he realised that he had some cigarettes in his pocket, so he went back to give those cigarettes to the other detainees, and when he arrived there, he said that the prison gates were open and there was no one in the prison. And one of the policemen asked him what he was looking for and he said, Well, I wanted to give them cigarettes and he replied, well, they won't need them anymore, they've had their final cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when did you learn what happened to the men who had been detained with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: The very next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: A Serb woman. Or, rather, she was a Croat, but she was married to a Serb. She came to tell me that I was lucky, that I was lucky to have survived, and she said that all the others had been shot about an hour later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember -- without telling me just yet, do you remember the names of the other people who were detained with you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I would ask that the court usher please call up 65 ter 5255.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I will ask you to look at this list and tell me if you know these people.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, can you read the names that you recognise and tell me where these people are from, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Ivan Andjal, Ivan Andjal was from Bilje in Baranja. Pavle Beck was in Erdut. Haso Brajic from Osijek. I don't know Zeljko Filipcic. As for this Ivan Florjan, he is from Bilje. Kusic is from Sotin. I don't know Radovanovic, where he is from. A Stimac person, I don't remember him. Zelember is from Batina, and he was the chairman of the HDZ there. And then Zemljak Pavao and his son Vladimir are from Beli Manastir in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what happened to these people?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, they were found dead in cells or in "celija."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the meaning.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... near Vinkovci, which means that they had been shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And are these the men that were detained with you then?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you said that some of them were from other places, so how was it -- how is it that you are able to remember their names and that you know where they are from?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: While we were in the prison in Dalj, the teacher or professor said, Who knows who is going to remain alive and who is going to get shot dead, so let us each ask each other every single day what our names and where we are from so that later on we can tell the families that so and so was killed in such and such place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I would now like to talk specifically about Arkan's men. You stated that you saw Arkan himself at the jail. Did you see him again in town?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when was the first time that you saw him and his men in town, or, sorry, in the village of Erdut?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I didn't see him in Erdut at all. I saw him in Dalj when he came and beat us in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you see his men in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you see them ever engage in any violent behaviour?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, their behaviour was always violent. They never behaved like human beings. A neighbour of mine who was there, they stood him against a wall of a house and then they shot at him with, what do you call it, they had darts, like darts, something like darts that they actually aimed at him and then he was bleeding all over, and he came over to my house and asked for some brandy so that he could actually wash out the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you personally see any of this, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: To your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Whom, what happened? Oh, I see. Well, no, I didn't, but he told me when once they were gone, I didn't dare go out because they would have shot me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you or your neighbour report this to the police, to Bozidar Bolic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, there was no point reporting this to anyone. I did not report this to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Why do you say that there was no point reporting it, just briefly? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, even the people who had incidents of that type and reported them, it didn't help them at all. Quite the contrary, on the next day they would come and beat him to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever try to get a permit to leave Erdut at some point between the time of your imprisonment but before you eventually managed to leave in February?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, before the Yugoslav Army arrived, my wife had a cataract and she had to go to Zagreb to have eye surgery, but when she went to Zagreb, the hospital was actually being renovated. So she was told that she would be called for surgery when the hospital was again operational, and then when this evil happened, she had some pain in her eyes, so I went up to them to ask for a permit in order to take my wife to the hospital. They wouldn't issue the permit to me because, as they said, I was not the list. Then I asked them what list? And they said, Well, you are on the list. Then I said, Well, let me take a look at it. Then they pulled it out of a drawer, they pulled out a list on which all Croats were, all the Croat names were on the list. And they wouldn't let me go. And it was only later on when we actually fled Erdut when we actually left Erdut that she could have eye surgery in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you about that time when you actually did managed to leave Erdut in February of 1992, why is it, or what prompted your decision to leave?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, one couldn't survive there anymore. Every other day I had to go to an office for questioning, and they always asked the same thing, and then they also came at night to my home, the troops, and then they searched, they searched our wardrobes and closets to make sure that no one was hidden there. We had no rights, we weren't given any food, any clothes, and we realised we couldn't survive there, that we had to flee.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sutalo for answering my questions. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Friedman. Could I inquire with the other parties how much time they would need for cross-examination so as to be able to fix the proper moment for our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: About ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, not more than 30 minutes, let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest, since we had a late start, that you cross-examine the witness for ten minutes, Mr. Jordash, that we then have a break and that we then hear the evidence of the witness when cross-examined by you, Mr. Bakrac. Yes, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intended to tender 65 ter 5255 which was the victim list from Dalj, and I believe I did not request to do so at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think you did. Any objections? I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, this witness list would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P00304, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P304 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Sutalo, we'll continue for another ten minutes, then we'll have a break, and then we'll hope to finish in the second session. Mr. Jordash. Mr. Sutalo, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I express my sympathy for your experience and indicate to you that I do not seek to challenge what happened to you or suggest it's not true, just so you know that -- where my questions are coming from. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you very few questions, and I'll take probably about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The first question I want to ask you is about this man Cizmic you mentioned, who was a police officer, is that right, at the Dalj police station?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he was the only police officer you recognised from before these events?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He was a police officer at the Dalj police station, is that right, before these events?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall whether his first name was Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you know him personally before the event, or did you simply know him by sight?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. I did know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What kind of police officer did you observe he was before the event? Are you able to offer any observations on that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, that depended on who you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that, please.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't a bad man but then when this whole unfortunate thing happened, he turned out to be not so good. But later on when the Croat -- he too came to the police force, became a member of the police force later on, the Croatian policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the last sentence. He became a member of the police force later on, the Croatian policeman, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but you see, when I came back, or rather when we were in Dalj, he told me that he would kill me and then put me in a hole two metres deep. In 1948 when I returned home, I had to go and report to the police station and say that I was in Erdut. When I arrived I saw him there, he was wearing a Croatian uniform, a uniform of Croatian police and then later on he returned. Where he had come from, I don't know. He had fled to Serbia, and then he came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mentioned the date 1948, did you mean to say 1948 in?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you knew Cizmic in 1948?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Not 1948, 1998. Before that I saw him he was a policeman in the Dalj police station, and then when he was on duty, I would see him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. You said about Cizmic that when this whole unfortunate thing happened, he turned out to be not so good. Let me ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did you observe him doing to make you come to that view?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: When I came to Dalj, when the police brought me, he -- one time I came outside to drink some water, and he saw me and said, What are you doing here? And I said, Well, I'm here. And then he said, Luka. And I said, Leave me alone, I just want to drink some water. But he wouldn't let me do that, and he said that I was going to go into the ground, two feet under. Two metres under.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just consult with my colleague, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let me try to take this chronologically. Again nothing you've said do I disagree with or seek to challenge, but I just want to try to make sure the Court understands what you are saying about Zeljko Cizmic. Did you see him when you went to police station in Dalj on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I saw him on a number of occasions in Dalj. He would come to the police station every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was he in a position of authority in the police station at Dalj?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to see that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did the event take place that you've just described where he refused to let you take a drink of water? Was that your first visit to Dalj police station on the 25th, or after you had been to the Borovo police station?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, when I returned two or three days after that, when we came back from Borovo, that's when it happened. I was wondering what was he saying to me when we knew each other and when we used to say hello to each other before. And then for him to become so brutal then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you say brutal about Mr. Cizmic? What was it you observed that made you --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Because he didn't let me have a drink of water and because he threatened to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did he order you back inside?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you observe him being brutal to other detainees?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't really able to notice that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know or did you hear from anyone else whether he had a reputation for brutality?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: All I know that Palinkas, there was something wrong with him too. We were the only ones -- he was from Aljmas, and I was from Erdut, it's the same area, the same municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to stay with Cizmic for a moment. You observed him being brutal to you, and I'm interested in whether you know or have heard whether he was brutal to anybody else during this period?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I heard that Palinkas also went somewhere and then he told him to go back as well, so I heard that about him in relation to Palinkas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Palinkas tried to leave the station and you heard that Cizmic told him to return inside likewise?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell him to go back inside, but he, himself, they had a kind of altercation. Palinkas's son was killed in the Croatian police and that's probably why they had a kind of argument, and that's why he shouted at him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Palinkas told you this directly, did he?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you observe Cizmic working alongside Arkan?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see him working alongside Milorad Stricevic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them together. He would go to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who would go to whose office?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Cizmic would go to Stricevic's offices, and Stricevic was the komandir of the police there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear anything to indicate to you that Zeljko Cizmic was anything other than an enthusiastic colleague of Milorad Stricevic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, they were on good terms, I saw that. I couldn't really notice that they were on bad terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What you observed was Cizmic working as a friendly, willing colleague of Colonel Stricevic, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Can I again consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something for the transcript, Mr. Witness. And I think it's my fault and my pronunciation, but I want to make sure that we are talking, you and I, about the same man. We are talking about -- all the questions I've just asked you and all the answers you've given about Zeljko concerned Zeljko Cizmic, C-i-z-m-i-c; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move -- sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I asked you 20 minutes ago, how much time you would need, you said ten minutes, I did this also in view of the well-being of your client. It now gave me the impression that you wanted to go to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I apologise for the bad -- for the poor approximation. I hadn't expected the witness to be able to deal with some of these issues, so everything took a bit longer. I've got about five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that would bring us to one hour and 25 minutes, if Mr. Stanisic would prefer to have the break now, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just check, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm on the stop clock, five minutes, please, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Continue, five minutes. I look at the clock and I'll -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to ask you about something you said in response to a question by prosecuting counsel when you first began today. And it concerns who was manning the check-points within -- within Erdut.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That was the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is the case, isn't it, Mr. Witness, that first when you spoke about who was manning the check-points, you said it was the JNA soldiers, when you first gave your statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No. Yes, but I -- that was my remark. That was my objection, that it wasn't the JNA, but the Serbian police there in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say the Serbian police, are you talking about local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you recognise some of them as local --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I recognised each one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness, no further questions from me. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Sutalo, we'll first take a break, and we'll resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For urgent personal reasons, Judge Gwaunza is unable to continue sitting at this moment. Judge Picard and myself, we have considered whether we are convinced that it's in the interest of justice to continue and hear the case, and we are convinced that it is, therefore, we'll continue. Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to cross-exam the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just like my learned friend, Mr. Jordash, I'm first going to express to you on behalf of my client and my team my regret and our regret for the unpleasant experiences that you went through.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have your statements before us, as well as your testimony in the Milosevic case. I do not wish to counter anything that you have said or to go into any kind of discussion with you relating to certain questions on which you were quite clear. I'm just going to have a few questions in order to clarify in more detail some things. May I begin, Mr. Sutalo?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, you may, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sutalo, your first experience with this military officer Kosutic, you said that he interrogated you at the Bogojevo factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, Bogojevo is the first settlement as soon as you cross the Danube from Croatia into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We can say it's only -- it's right at the --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Right at the border, at the bank of the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were interrogated by this Mr. Kosutic, if I understood you correctly, you were taken there by a certain Zvonko Tucak from Erdut and a certain person -- another person, Mata, who was from Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, he was from Dalj. Actually, he was working in Dalj, and he was born in Vojvodina, and he lived there. It's just that once he got work in Dalj, he stayed there, and this is where this misfortune overtook him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, and these are the two people who called you out as Sutalo and took you to this military officer Kosutic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, you talked about Marko Loncarevic and you said in your statement in paragraph 21, and it's on page 4 both in the English and the B/C/S versions, that he was from Dalj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Dalj is in Croatia, isn't it, right next to Erdut; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, in the Milosevic case, transcript 22572 [sic], you said that Marko Loncarevic, about whom you are not sure as to what position he had, what job he was doing, was in charge of everything. He was asked about everything, is this correct, this Marko Loncarevic from Dalj?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, Marko Loncarevic from Dalj. During that meeting, Jovo -- I used to know his last name, but I can't remember it right now. He said, What are you going to do with the wheat? Because it was harvest time, and the -- you couldn't -- the transport was interrupted at Bijelo Brdo, the Serbs had cut it off, so you couldn't bring that in any more. So the question was, Jovo, what are you going to do with the wheat? And then somebody said Osijek has paid for the wheat, the wheat has to go to Osijek. And then Loncarevic said, This is no longer Croatia; this is Serbia; the wheat has to go to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. I understood, so this Loncarevic who was born in Dalj and who was from Dalj from Croatia from your neighbourhood, that was him; right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, in order to avoid confusion at a later stage, you referred, at least that was how it was translated, to page 22572 - 22572 - where apparently you wanted to refer to 25572.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 25572, Your Honours. I think that's what I said, if I misspoke, perhaps, then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not blaming anyone, it's not worth while finding out, but I'm just trying to avoid that at later stage people have to make a huge effort to find the right page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, in your statement you also say that a few days after the invasion, a large number of Serbs from Erdut, local Serbs, joined the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You even mentioned their names and you said that those persons who joined the police, the local Serbs who joined the police started by stealing property from abandoned homes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, you also mentioned a certain Milorad Gogic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain what his duties were. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: All I know is that he was a looter and that he had the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army. He wore a police uniform. And he also had a uniform of Arkan's Chetniks. I don't know what he was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And this Milorad Gogic, was he from Dalj or Erdut?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: He was born in Bosnia and he came to this area as a child. His mother, Mileva, brought him, and he lived right next door to me. His house was some 10 metres away from my house, right next to my house. During these unfortunate events, he had four cisterns in his yard, three cars, and one loader. I said, Where did you get a loader, for God's sake? And he said from -- from Sarvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sutalo.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You told me about forced labour, or you talked about forced labour. Can you please tell me if it's correct that forced labour was a decision made by some local body?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that this was the military training camp, and this is where the young men went for their training. And this is where we went to clear the old branches, to mow the grass, and clear it away. It was very neglected. And I was given the summons by a certain Darko Perepovic [phoen]. He brought me the summons, and the summons was signed by Bolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, a lot of time has gone by, you said that Dejan Djakovic came to you with the order or summons signed by Bolic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, could I ask you to just make a short break between question and answer because you speak the same language, and then we often have overlapping speakers, and your words might be lost if the interpreters cannot translate it for you -- for us. So, therefore, could you try to make a break, and Mr. Bakrac will give a good example by doing the same, to just pause for a second once you've given your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I hope that you heard what His Honour, the presiding judge said, I'm going to try, and I will ask you also, to try to make a break. So the order on the labour duty was signed by Bolic, Bozidar Bolic was in charge of the local police, the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And now tell me something about another person, about Milorad Stricevic, you testified about him. Who was that? Can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know, he was from Dalj, and I am from Erdut. All I know is that when I arrived the first evening he was the person in charge there, and he had a policeman with him who had a whip. And some people said later that he was actually a driver; he wasn't a lieutenant. I don't know what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the transcript, when you say from Dalj, does that mean that he was a local Serb from the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, you testified about your son, or rather, about how he came to the police station and brought some things and cigarettes for you, and so on. This was not quite clear from your testimony in the Milosevic case and from your statement, so can we clarify that. Your son, Vidoje, was he a member of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the English page 7, I believe that's paragraph 41, and it begins with, "Vidoje my elder son is married it to Marinka, she had a relative in the JNA," and so on. As for the transcript page in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I was asking for primarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me a moment, Your Honours, I jotted it down. That's 25578. Page 25578.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, it is unclear and I would appreciate it if you could clarify it now, and if you cannot, that's also all right, but tell us, your son Vidoje, was he a member?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: My son Vidoje is married to Marinka Milojkovic, a Serb, and he, too, was with the Serbian army that went to defend Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, your son Vidoje was in the Serb Krajina army; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I have just a few other questions and I believe that I will be done in five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Oh, just go ahead, I have plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, I know that, Mr. Sutalo, but I think because we are doing this well, we are moving along fast. So I will have just another question about this. You mentioned in your statement a certain Milenko Simic. And where you said that the local people began to disappear and their wives and relatives, that Milenko Simic was actually involved in that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Milenko Simic was a Serb policeman. He drove a Serb police car, and he went, I don't know who he received orders from, but he went to collect the people as ordered. And whenever he drove someone, that someone never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, let's just be precise, when you say a member of the Serb police, you mean the local Serb police? He was a local man?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There was an incident where a hand-grenade was actually lobbed into your garden and you said that you reported this to a Trolic or a Trovic, could you tell us who this person was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, that was the chief commander of the JNA, the army that went to Vukovar and returned from the battle-field, and he was -- actually his staff was in the house of my son, and I reported this incident with the hand-grenade. This was 15 minutes before Christmas when this happened and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear who it was who threw the bomb, the hand-grenade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, the interpreters could not hear who it was that threw the hand-grenade. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hand-grenade or who it was who title threw it, I don't know. But I know that it was one of his policemen, but they wouldn't say who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, isn't it correct that after you returned to Erdut, you heard that this hand-grenade was actually thrown by a local policeman, Zoran Oljaca?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, Gogic told me about it, but he said that it wasn't him but the other one, but now I don't really know which one. When you don't see something, you can't really confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, the permit to leave Erdut, you requested to be issued this permit -- you requested Mr. Bolic, correct, the commander of the police in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: In Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Erdut. Now, you said that in order to obtain the permit, you had to actually sign over your house and your property to the village council. Now, what I would like -- please listen to my question carefully. Once you returned after the JNA retreated, was your property still in the registry of deeds? Was it still registered there under your name?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, my house was registered in the registry in Osijek, and at this time it was impossible to go from Krajina to Osijek in order to enter the information, so my house remained -- the deed on my house remained in my name, and this was true not only for my house, but for everyone else who actually signed over their property, because those signatures weren't worth anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sutalo. Now, tell me one more thing. Was there a certain number of people of Croat nationality who remained in Erdut after you left and remained there all through until you returned?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's true. Many people stayed back, but not I returned, because about 20 days later all Croats left Erdut. Everyone was expelled, so that in fact Erdut remained ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they all request to be issued permits to leave?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it was they sought. They must have because the Serb police did not allow anyone who hadn't signed over their property to them. No one was allowed to leave unless they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, you all crossed over to Serbia and then from there you moved on?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, the last group of Croats who were expelled, were expelled via -- or they had to cross Bijelo Brdo on then on to Osijek. But the earlier group, when we fled, we fled via Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, at this time when a large number of Croats left that area, was there a large influx of refugees from Serbian Krajina following in the after math of Oluja and Pakrac? Was it -- were they expected -- were they waiting for a large number of refugees, of Serb refugees to come over from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know, but I know that a large number of Serbs did come, and they were -- later on they were given the Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sutalo. Now, could we just go back to the very beginning of your statement, I just wanted to make sure about something there. In paragraph 3 of your statement which then became Exhibit P301, you said prior to the elections in 1990, relations between the different ethnic groups in Erdut were almost perfect. We all had good relations with each other, attending each other's weddings, funerals, and feasts. This was due in part to the many mixed marriages. And then you go on explain that when the HDZ party was established, you became a member of it. Now, my question, Mr. Sutalo, is this -- and as a member I'm sure you must have known, and I suppose that you will agree with me, but the basic policy, the underlying policy of the HDZ was to secede from Yugoslavia, for Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, everything went on well until Jovo Raskovic came along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Sutalo --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Your Honours, we have this in the testimony in the Milosevic case. I don't want to cover the same ground; I just want to put a very specific question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until Raskovic's speech in Dalj, everything was all right, but from that moment on, the Serbs began to avoid speaking with us, and then all of this happened. We were never told by anyone in the HDZ that we should part ways or that you have to listen to our orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I fully understand what you are saying, but please let's try and focus in order to finish as soon as we can. So please listen to my question carefully, and it's very simple. I am not asking about who showed what. But just tell me, is it true that the policy of the HDZ was for Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia and to establish Croatia as an independent state? That is my first question.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No one ever said that in any meeting or any gathering. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that when the HDZ came to power, the Serb people, which until then, had been an constituent ethnic group in Croatia, now lost this feature and became a national minority, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Of the Serbs in Erdut, and there were 23 per cent of them, no one ever touched them. No one ever gave them a bad look. No one ever hit them, and they killed 35 Croats in Erdut, and now you draw your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I understand what you are saying fully. And I'm not saying that in Erdut or in Dalj you resorted to violence or that you treated the Serbs, your neighbours, improperly. My question only is this. When the HDZ came into power, the Serb people, who until then figured as a constituent ethnic group, were now expelled from that, or no longer had that position.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't read the constitution, and I've never read anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Sutalo, on the first page of your statement, paragraph 4, you say, The HDZ party was formed, I became a member. And then your meetings were held in Stjepan Lucan's house in Orasje on the outskirts of Erdut. My question is why does a legally established party meet in a private home on the outskirts of Erdut, rather than meet in the culture centre in Erdut which probably existed, so why was this happening in a private home on the outskirts of Erdut?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, there was no culture centre, nor were the meetings held there because it didn't exist. Now later on when Arkan came, he actually built a large culture centre and also the same happened in the village a bit further on, so now we have two of them in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't there -- weren't there any premises where a meeting of a party could be held publicly at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, the meetings were actually convened by the chairman of the HDZ board, and I don't know why he chose to convene them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know when the new constitution was adopted in Croatia when the HDZ came to power, that members of the police of Serb ethnicity were forced to leave the police?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Erdut and Dalj.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, to this day there are five or six police officers of Serb ethnicity in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I believe we did not understand each other. I'm not talking about the present time. I'm talking about the period that is relevant for this case. I'm talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's all right. Now, I have a few more questions. You mentioned on several occasions, as you testified, the word 'Chetniks.' You used that word. Now, tell me, sir, you are an elderly man, can you tell me whether the term "Chetnik" is a equally offensive as the term "Ustasha"?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I think so, they are both the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my final question, Mr. Sutalo, today, for the first time, you mentioned when speaking about Arkan's men. In other words, you gave a statement in 1999, you were questioned in the Milosevic case, and yet it is only today for the first time -- whereas even during the proofing sessions with my learned colleague, you never mentioned this. But you said today in your testimony that Arkan's men were actually -- had actually been released from juvenile detention facilities. Now, tell me this, all these years later, how is it that you've just mentioned this today and that you learned of this now?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I was a beekeeper and people would come to my place to buy honey from me. Most of these people were young people and then one of them said to me that most of these young men were actually -- or had actually been released from juvenile facilities so that they could actually March in Croatia. So that's where I learned that, and that's why I used that today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
